prompt: In `Walk.java`, what happened when `next()` was called after `hasNext()` had answered `false`?
hint: The last line of the program.

choices.text: It started again from `Dune`, at the head of the list
choices.why: An iterator never resets; a new walk needs a new iterator.

choices.text: It returned `null`, as the end-of-walk value
choices.why: Returning `null` is the queue's `poll`; an iterator's `next` throws.

choices.text: It threw `NoSuchElementException`
choices.why: Right: from `ImmutableCollections$ListItr.next`, the iterator `List.of` made.

prompt: `javap -c Shelf` showed three interface calls for one `for-each` loop. Which were they?
hint: The loop asks the list for something first.

choices.text: `List.size`, `List.get` and `String.length`
choices.why: Those would be an index loop; `for-each` on a list never calls `get`.

choices.text: `List.iterator`, `Iterator.hasNext` and `Iterator.next`
choices.why: Right: the compiler rewrote the loop into the iterator protocol.

choices.text: `Iterable.forEach`, called once with the loop body
choices.why: That method exists, but the bytecode shows the three calls of an ordinary loop.

choices.text: A single `foreach` instruction of the JVM, with two helper calls
choices.why: There is no such instruction; the JVM only sees calls.

prompt: A `for-each` loop compiles over an array, or over anything that implements the interface `___`.
Why can you not write `for (var e : map)` directly over a `Map`?

choices.text: `Map` is not `Iterable`; you walk a view
choices.why: Right: `keySet()`, `values()` or `entrySet()`, each of which is iterable.

choices.text: Maps can only be read by key, with `get`
choices.why: They can be walked; only not directly, as a `Map`.

choices.text: A map's order is undefined, so Java forbids iterating it
choices.why: `TreeMap` has a defined order and still is not `Iterable`; the reason is the interface.

prompt: Two loops each call `shelf.iterator()` on the same list. The first loop is halfway through when the second starts. Where does the second one begin?

choices.text: Halfway, where the first one is
choices.why: The position belongs to each iterator, not to the list.

choices.text: Before the first element, with a position of its own
choices.why: Right: each call to `iterator()` makes a new object with its own position.

choices.text: It throws `ConcurrentModificationException`, since two iterators are open
choices.why: Reading with two iterators changes nothing; only a structural change trips the check.

prompt: Why did the exception in `Walk.java` name a class, `ImmutableCollections$ListItr`, that the program never mentions?

choices.text: Because `Walk` declared its own iterator class without naming it
choices.why: `Walk` declares no class but itself; the iterator came from the list.

choices.text: Because `List.of` returns a list that cannot be walked
choices.why: It was walked perfectly; the exception came only after the end.

choices.text: That is the iterator class of `List.of`'s lists
choices.why: Right: `iterator()` returned an object of a JDK class written for that list.

prompt: `Overdue.java` removed an element from `loans` inside a `for-each` over `loans`. What happened?

choices.text: `ConcurrentModificationException`, on the next `next()`
choices.why: Right: the list had changed behind the iterator.

choices.text: It printed `[Dune, Ulysses, Beloved]`
choices.why: It never reached the `println`.

choices.text: It would not compile
choices.why: It compiled; the failure happened at run time.

prompt: `Overdue.java` has one thread. Why is the exception called *Concurrent*ModificationException?
hint: Two things were changing or reading the list at once.

choices.text: Because the JVM starts a hidden thread to run every `for-each`
choices.why: No thread is started; the loop runs in `main`'s thread.

choices.text: Two ways of using one list overlapped: the walk and the `remove`
choices.why: Right: one thread, two ways of changing or walking the list at once.

choices.text: Because the garbage collector moved the list during the loop
choices.why: The collector moving objects is invisible to programs; the count of changes is what differed.

prompt: How does an `ArrayList` iterator know the list changed behind it?

choices.text: It keeps a copy of every element and compares them on each `next()`
choices.why: That would double the memory; it keeps one number.

choices.text: The list sends it a message whenever `remove` is called
choices.why: Lists do not track their iterators; the iterator checks.

choices.text: It compares the list's `modCount` with the value it copied
choices.why: Right: a difference on `next()` means a structural change happened.

prompt: `Quiet.java` removed `Ulysses:late` inside the loop and finished with no exception. What went wrong?

choices.text: Nothing: the check only fires when the removed element is the first
choices.why: It removed one late loan and left another in the list, which is wrong.

choices.text: `remove` failed silently and `Ulysses:late` is still in the list
choices.why: The printed list has no `Ulysses:late`; it was removed.

choices.text: `hasNext()` stopped early, so the loop never checked `Beloved:late` at all
choices.why: Right: `hasNext()` saw the cursor equal to the size and stopped, after three `checking` lines for four loans.

prompt: In the figure, after `Ulysses:late` was removed, the cursor was 3. What was the list's size?
Inside a `for-each` over an `ArrayList`, which of these does not trip the fail-fast check?

choices.text: `list.add(x)`
choices.why: Adding changes the structure and moves `modCount`.

choices.text: `list.set(i, x)`
choices.why: Right: replacing an element is not a structural change.

choices.text: `list.remove(x)`
choices.why: Removing is the change section 03 tripped on.

choices.text: `list.clear()`
choices.why: Clearing removes every element, a structural change.

prompt: Which call removes every loan ending in `:late` from `b` without writing a loop?

choices.text: `b.removeAll(":late")`
choices.why: `removeAll` takes a collection of elements to remove, not a pattern.

choices.text: `b.removeIf(loan -> loan.endsWith(":late"))`
choices.why: Right: it walks the list itself, safely.

choices.text: `b.remove(":late")`
choices.why: That removes an element equal to the string `:late`, and there is none.

prompt: Why does `it.remove()` not cause the exception that `loans.remove(loan)` caused?

choices.text: `it.remove()` only marks it; the list removes it later
choices.why: It removes it at once; the printed list after the loop had no late loans.

choices.text: The iterator made the change, so it updates its own count and cursor
choices.why: Right: the change no longer happens behind its back.

choices.text: Because an explicit `Iterator` is not checked, only a `for-each` is
choices.why: The `for-each` uses the same iterator; the difference is who removes.

prompt: The `ListIterator` loop turned four loans into seven elements. Why did it not then visit the letters it had inserted?
hint: Where does `add` put the new element?

choices.text: Because `add` puts new elements at the end of the list
choices.why: The letters sit right after each fined loan, not at the end.

choices.text: It did visit them, and skipped them since they do not end in `:late`
choices.why: They would have been skipped by the `if`, but `next()` never returned them at all.

choices.text: `add` puts it behind the cursor, out of `next()`'s way
choices.why: Right: the iterator walks on from after the insertion.

prompt: Match each need to the technique the section's table gives for it.

pairs.left: Decide element by element, with a side effect
Replace or insert while walking a list
Call a method that changes the list from inside the loop

prompt: A loop over `member.loans()` calls `member.returnLoan(loan)`, which removes the loan from that same list inside `Member`. Which technique fits?
hint: The loop cannot reach the iterator that would have to remove.

choices.text: An explicit `Iterator` and `it.remove()`
choices.why: The removal happens inside `returnLoan`, not through your iterator.

choices.text: Walk a copy, `List.copyOf(member.loans())`
choices.why: Right: the copy does not change, and `returnLoan` changes the real list freely.

choices.text: A `ListIterator`, so that the removal is allowed
choices.why: A list iterator only protects changes it makes itself.

choices.text: Catch `ConcurrentModificationException` and continue the loop
choices.why: The check is best-effort; catching it hides a bug that may also skip elements.

prompt: Put the steps of a `for-each` over a list in the order the compiled code does them.
items: Call `next()` and assign the loop variable

prompt: A program catches `ConcurrentModificationException` around its loop and logs it, "just in case". What does section 03 say is wrong with that?

choices.text: The exception is an `Error`, and an `Error` cannot be caught by a `catch` block
choices.why: It is an ordinary `RuntimeException` and can be caught; the problem is relying on it.

choices.text: The check is best-effort, and `Quiet.java`'s bug threw nothing
choices.why: Right: `Quiet.java` was wrong and threw nothing to catch.

choices.text: Logging is slow, and the loop should be fast
choices.why: Speed is not the issue; correctness is.

prompt: Which of these change a `HashMap` safely while walking it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Through the view, or not at all.

choices.text: `map.entrySet().removeIf(e -> e.getValue() == 0)`
choices.why: Yes: the view walks and removes, and removing from a view removes from the map.

choices.text: A `for-each` over `map.keySet()` calling `map.remove(key)`
choices.why: That is section 03's mistake, through a map.

choices.text: An iterator over `map.values()` calling `it.remove()`
choices.why: Yes: the change is made by the iterator that walks.

choices.text: A `for-each` over `map.entrySet()` calling `map.put` with a new key
choices.why: Adding a key is a structural change made outside the iterator.
